narrative:
Your application was reviewed by a predictive model that assessed your likelihood of passing the bar exam on the first attempt, and the model estimated a 51.8% probability that you would not pass — a result that sits right on the edge of the decision boundary, meaning your situation is genuinely close to the threshold for approval. Because the model predicted you would fail, your application was unfortunately rejected. It is important to understand that this decision was based on academic and background factors, and notably, your gender and racial background played no role in the model's assessment.

To help explain what drove this outcome, it is useful to think about "what if" scenarios — alternative versions of your profile that would have been enough to flip the prediction from "will fail" to "will pass." These scenarios don't describe what you must do perfectly, but rather reveal which aspects of your profile the model is most sensitive to, and therefore where change would matter most.

The model generated three such alternative scenarios, and the pattern across all three is remarkably consistent: in every single case, only one feature changed, and it was the same one — your undergraduate GPA. In all three counterfactuals, no other factor shifted at all. Your first-year law school decile ranking, your third-year decile ranking, your LSAT score, your family income bracket, and your full-time enrollment status all remained exactly as they are in your actual profile. This tells a clear story: the model's tipping point for your application hinges almost entirely on your undergraduate GPA.

Currently, your undergraduate GPA stands at 3.40, which is actually slightly above the average of 3.24 among students who passed the bar exam in the dataset. At first glance, this might seem like a strength, and in isolation it is — but the model appears to be weighing it in combination with other signals in your profile. Specifically, your first-year law school decile of 2 and third-year decile of 1 are considerably below the averages of roughly 6 for students who passed, and these in-school performance indicators seem to be pulling the prediction toward failure. The counterfactuals suggest that a modest downward adjustment in your undergraduate GPA — on average just 0.2 points lower, bringing it to around 3.2 — would, paradoxically, shift the model's overall assessment in your favor.

This counterintuitive finding likely reflects a pattern the model learned from historical data: students with a very high undergraduate GPA relative to their in-law-school performance may represent a particular risk profile, perhaps suggesting that the transition to law school has been more challenging than their prior academic record would predict. In other words, the gap between your undergraduate performance and your law school decile rankings may be what the model is reacting to. Your LSAT score of 36 is close to the average of 37.27 among students who passed, and your full-time enrollment aligns with the vast majority of successful students, so these are not the areas of concern.

The most actionable takeaway here is that your in-law-school academic performance — particularly your class rankings in years one and three — appears to be the deeper driver of the model's concern, even though those features did not change in the counterfactuals. Since your undergraduate GPA cannot realistically be changed retroactively, the practical path forward is to focus on improving your law school standing, as stronger decile rankings in future assessments would likely shift the overall picture in your favor. Seeking academic support, forming study groups, or working with faculty advisors to strengthen your performance in law school coursework would be the most meaningful steps you could take to improve your prospects on the bar exam and, by extension, your application outcome.
